# completeness {.divider}


::: {style="border: 2px solid #7f8c8d; background: #f8f9fa; padding: 0.5em 1em; border-radius: 6px; margin-top: 1.2em;"}
For all sets of formulas $\Gamma$ and formula $\varphi$, 

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Gamma \nvdash \varphi &  &\Gamma \not \models \varphi\\
\ \ \Updownarrow &  & \ \ \Updownarrow \\
\Gamma, \neg \varphi \ \textsf{consistent} & \Rightarrow & \Gamma, \neg \varphi \ \textsf{satisfiable} \\
\end{array}
$$

For all sets of formulas $\Gamma$,

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
\Gamma  \ \textsf{consistent} & \Rightarrow & \Gamma \ \textsf{satisfiable} \\
\end{array}
$$
:::


## the plan 

Given a consistent set $\Gamma$, we will explain how to expand it into a *maximal consistent* set $\Sigma$.


<br/>
<br/>

# three arrows {.divider}

## left arrow: Lindenbaum {.smaller}

$$\begin{array}{clllc}
 \color{#7a003c}{\Gamma  \ \text{consistent}} & & & &  \Gamma \ \text{satisfiable}\\
 \color{#7a003c}{\Downarrow} & & & & \Uparrow \\
 \color{#7a003c}{\Gamma \subseteq \Sigma \ \text{and} \ \Sigma \ \text{maximal consistent}} & & \Rightarrow & &   \Gamma \subseteq \Sigma \ \text{and} \ \Sigma \  \ \text{satisfiable}\\ 
\end{array}$$

. . .

::: {.theorem}
**Lindenbaum theorem**. If $\Gamma$ is *consistent*, then $\Gamma$ is a subset of a *maximal consistent* set $\Sigma$.
:::

. . .

::: {.proof}
Enumerate all the formulas of propositional logic 

$$
\varphi_0, \varphi_1, \varphi_2, \dots
$$ 
and build a chain

$$
\Gamma = \Sigma_0 \subseteq \Sigma_1 \subseteq \Sigma_2 \subseteq \cdots
$$
where $\Sigma_{0}$ is $\Gamma$ and $\Sigma_{n+1}$ is $\Sigma_n, \varphi_n$ if *consistent*, and $\Sigma_n$ otherwise. 

Let $\Sigma = \bigcup_n \Sigma_n$. Notice that the identity of $\Sigma$ is very sensitive to the details of the enumeration. 
:::

## Lindenbaum Theorem {.smaller}

Let $\varphi_0, \varphi_1, \dots$ be an *enumeration* of the formulas of propositional logic.

Define a chain $\Sigma_0 \subseteq \Sigma_1 \subseteq \Sigma_2 \subseteq \cdots$ by the recursion:

$$\begin{array}{lll}
\Sigma_0 &  = &  \Gamma \\
\Sigma_{n+1} & = & \begin{cases} \Sigma_n, \varphi_n & \text{if consistent}\\ \Sigma_n &  \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\end{array}$$

::: {.theorem}
1. $\Gamma \subseteq \Sigma$
2. For each natural number $n$ $\Sigma_n$ is consistent.
3. For each natural number $n$, for every $m < n$, $\Sigma_m \subseteq \Sigma_n$.
4. For every finite subset $\Delta \subseteq \Sigma$, there is some natural number $n$ such that $\Delta \subseteq \Sigma_n$.
5. $\Sigma$ is consistent.
6. $\Sigma$ is maximal consistent.
:::


## Lindenbaum Lemma {.smaller}

::: {.theorem}
2. For each natural number $n$ $\Sigma_n$ is consistent.
:::

::: {.proof}
Induction on $n$. 

- *$\Sigma_0$ is consistent*. $\Sigma_0$ is just $\Gamma$, which we have assumed to be consistent.

- *If $\Sigma_n$ is consistent, then so is $\Sigma_{n+1}$*. Suppose $\Sigma_n$ is consistent. Then $\Sigma_{n+1}$ is either $\Sigma_n, \varphi_n$ if consistent, or $\Sigma_n$, otherwise. Either way, $\Sigma_{n+1}$ is consistent.
:::

::: {.theorem}
3. For each natural number $n$, for every $m < n$, $\Sigma_m \subseteq \Sigma_n$.
::: 

::: {.proof}
Induction on $n$.

- *for every $m < 0$, $\Sigma_n \subseteq \Sigma_0$*. Trivial.

- *If for every $m < n$, $\Sigma_m \subseteq \Sigma_n$, then for every $m < n +1$, $\Sigma_m \subseteq \Sigma_{n+1}$*. By construction, $\Sigma_n \subseteq \Sigma_{n+1}$. So, if $m \leq n$, then $\Sigma_m \subseteq \Sigma_n \subseteq \Sigma_{n+1}$.
:::

## Lindenbaum Lemma {.smaller}

::: {.theorem}
4. For every finite subset $\Delta \subseteq \Sigma$, there is some natural number $n$ such that $\Delta \subseteq \Sigma_n$.
:::

::: {.proof}
Given a finite subset $\Delta$ of $\Sigma$, let $\varphi_n$ be the member of $\Delta$ of highest index. Then $\Delta \subseteq \Sigma_{n+1}$.
:::

::: {.theorem}
5. $\Sigma$ is consistent.
:::

::: {.proof}
For a reductio, suppose $\Sigma \vdash \bot$. Then there is a finite derivation of $\bot$ from $\Sigma$. So, there is a derivation of $\bot$ from a *finite* subset $\Delta$ of $\Sigma$, making $\Delta$ inconsistent. But we showed that *every* finite subset of $\Sigma$ is consistent.
:::

::: {.theorem}
6. $\Sigma$ is maximal consistent.
:::

::: {.proof}
If $\varphi$ is a formula, then it has an index in the enumeration, namely, $\varphi$ is $\varphi_n$. So, if $\Sigma_n, \varphi_n$ is consistent, then $\varphi \in \Sigma_{n+1} \subseteq \Sigma$.
:::

## middle arrow: from maximal consistency to satisfiability {.smaller}

$$\begin{array}{clllc}
 \Gamma  \ \text{consistent} & & & &  \Gamma \ \text{satisfiable}\\
 \Downarrow & & & & \Uparrow \\
 \color{#7a003c}{\Gamma \subseteq \Sigma \ \text{and} \ \Sigma \ \text{maximal consistent}} & & \color{#7a003c}{\Rightarrow} & &   \color{#7a003c}{\Gamma \subseteq \Sigma \ \text{and} \ \Sigma \ \text{satisfiable}}\\ 
\end{array}$$

. . .

::: {.theorem}
**Henkin lemma.** If $\Sigma$ is *maximal consistent*, then $\Sigma$ is *satisfiable*.
:::

. . . 

::: {.proof}

Given a maximally consistent $\Sigma$, define the *canonical* assignment:

$$
\begin{array}{lll}
v_\Sigma(p) = 1 & \text{iff } & p \in \Sigma
\end{array}
$$
We use an induction on the complexity of formulas to prove:
$$
\begin{array}{lll}
V_\Sigma(\varphi) = 1 & \text{iff } & \varphi \in \Sigma
\end{array}
$$
:::

## Henkin Lemma {.smaller}


::: {.proof}
Induction on the complexity of formulas:

$$
\begin{array}{lllll}
\text{Base case}: & & & & \\
&V_\Sigma(p) = 1 & \text{iff } & v_\Sigma(p) = 1 & \\
& & \text{iff } & \varphi \in \Sigma & \textsf{definition of} \ v_\Sigma \\[8pt]
\text{Induction step for }  \neg\textbf{:} & & & & \\
& V_\Sigma(\neg \varphi) = 1 & \text{iff } & V_\Sigma(\varphi) = 0 & \textsf{definition of} \ V_\Sigma \\
& & \text{iff } & \varphi \notin \Sigma & \textsf{inductive hypothesis} \\
& & \text{iff } & \neg \varphi \in \Sigma & \textsf{maximal consistency} \\[8pt]
\text{Induction step for } \to\textbf{:} & & & & \\
& V_\Sigma(\varphi \to \psi) = 1 & \text{iff } & V_\Sigma(\varphi) = 0 \ \text{or} \ V_\Sigma(\psi) = 1 & \textsf{definition of} \ V_\Sigma \\
& & \text{iff } & \varphi \notin \Sigma \ \text{or} \ \psi \in \Sigma & \textsf{inductive hypothesis} \\
& & \text{iff } & \varphi \to \psi \in \Sigma & \textsf{maximal consistency} \\
\end{array}
$$
:::



## right arrow: monotonicity

$$\begin{array}{clllc}
 \Gamma  \ \text{consistent} & & & & \color{#7a003c}{\Gamma \ \text{satisfiable}}\\
 \Downarrow & & & & \color{#7a003c}{\Uparrow} \\
\Gamma \subseteq \Sigma \ \text{and} \ \Sigma  \ \text{maximal consistent} & &  \Rightarrow & &   \color{#7a003c}{\Gamma \subseteq \Sigma \ \text{and} \ \Sigma \ \text{satisfiable}}\\ 
\end{array}$$

. . .

If a valuation $V_\Sigma$ satisfies $\Sigma$ and $\Gamma$ is a *subset* of $\Sigma$, then $V$ satisfies $\Gamma$.


# summary {.divider}

## the proof

$$\begin{array}{clllc}
 \Gamma  \ \text{consistent} & & & & \Gamma \ \text{satisfiable}\\
  \Downarrow \ \text{\scriptsize Lindenbaum}  & & & & \Uparrow \ \text{\scriptsize monotonicity} \\
  \Gamma \subseteq \Sigma \ \text{and} \ \Sigma  \ \text{maximal consistent}) & & \underset{\text{\scriptsize Henkin lemma}}{\Rightarrow} & &   \Gamma \subseteq \Sigma \ \text{and} \ \Sigma   \ \text{satisfiable}\\ 
\end{array}$$

. . .

::: {.theorem}
**Completeness.** If a set $\Gamma$ is consistent, then $\Gamma$ is satisfiable. 
:::
